source.title: TwinBreak: Jailbreaking LLM Security Alignments based on Twin Prompts
source.authors: T. Krauß; Hamid Dashtbani; Alexandra Dmitrienko

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates directional ablation as a comparator, applying the refusal-direction intervention and measuring harmful-response outcomes across models. It also tests a different parameter-pruning removal method.
record.gate_note: The paper's own TwinBreak method identifies and prunes model parameters using activation differences for paired harmful and harmless prompts; it does not test the original difference-in-means residual-stream direction or adding that direction. It evaluates directional ablation as a comparison method. The paper reports unpruned baselines and utility-task results, but no result for adding a refusal direction.
record.test_reason: TwinBreak is a parameter-pruning method, not the difference-in-means direction. But the paper runs directional ablation (Arditi et al.) as a comparator on 16 models and reports ASR and StrongREJECT plus utility. These results bear on V1 and V6. The TwinBreak pruning results bear on V2 only loosely, since pruning is not an ablation-to-weight-edit.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly right: TwinBreak removes alignment by pruning with high ASR and small utility loss, and directional ablation is effective on many models but fails on Gemma 2 27B and Gemma 3 1B. The paper's main conclusion is about TwinBreak and does not test the refusal-direction claim itself. It treats Arditi et al. as a baseline and says its underlying intuition is somewhat unclear.
record.recipe_differences: TwinBreak uses paired similar prompts to identify and iteratively prune model parameters, rather than finding a harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream direction and projecting it out. The paper separately evaluates directional ablation [4] as a comparator.
record.method_sensitivity: For TwinBreak, results vary with pruning iteration, targeted MLP components, token selection, utility-parameter retention, pruning rate, and whether harmful/harmless prompts are matched as twins. The paper reports 7% lower ASR and utility loss up to 8.4% when using non-twin prompts; pruning Gate and Up together is more effective than pruning either alone. Directional-ablation results vary by model, with failures reported for Gemma 2 27B and Gemma 3 1B.

fits_no_version.finding: TwinBreak targeted pruning of Gate/Up MLP parameters, using twin-prompt activation differences, raises ASR to 94-99% across four models and StrongREJECT to 0.67-0.81 across 16 models with small utility loss. It is a different mechanism from a single residual-stream direction. It suggests refusal can also be removed by sparse parameter edits.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety alignment can be removed by pruning a small set of MLP parameters (about 5%) found from activation differences on paired harmful/harmless prompts.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says code and the dataset would be open-sourced after acceptance.
record.problems: No uncertainty intervals or significance tests are reported for the relevant results. The directional-ablation comparison does not provide matched unablated ASR values in its comparison tables. StrongREJECT scores are not refusal rates, and the larger-model directional-ablation table reports those scores without an explicit unablated comparison. TwinBreak's main evaluation often uses the pruned model for the first 50 tokens and then switches back to the unpruned model.
record.rows_left_out: No results-bearing rows omitted. Tables 3–5 and 21 report additional harmful-prompt datasets and StrongREJECT outcomes for the same four primary models; retained the HarmBench validation ASRs and the cross-model StrongREJECT results most directly relevant to the listed versions.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal; whether the direction is a single difference-in-means vector; whether other abilities beyond five multiple-choice benchmarks are kept. The paper runs the original method as a black box.

The abliteration weight-orthogonalisation edit itself is not tested. The paper's directional ablation is applied as activation intervention across all tokens and layers, and its pruning method is a different weight edit.
Transfer across languages, base to instruct models, or reuse of a direction between variants. The paper recomputes the direction separately per model.

missing.what: Matched unablated baselines for directional ablation. Table 5/8 gives them (e.g. LLaMA 2 7B 0.017) but the rows do not use them.
Directional ablation on JailbreakBench and AdvBench, and its utility on RTE, ARC, OpenBookQA and WinoGrande.
Utility costs for directional ablation on several models. HellaSwag drops of -33.0% (Gemma 3 1B), -18.5% (Gemma 2 27B) and -6.5% (Gemma 2 2B) appear in Table 8.
Authors' claim that TwinBreak beats directional ablation, with 4x lower runtime. Average StrongREJECT is 0.744 against 0.578.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The record's V2 support label, built from TwinBreak rows, should be dropped, since TwinBreak is not abliteration. The V6 support label is also weak: the direction is recomputed per model, which does not test transfer. I therefore give no V6 label. The Gemma 0.000 failures may be implementation or search failures of the comparator, not clear counterevidence, so the V1 challenge is limited to that recipe. Table 8 and Table 25 disagree for LLaMA 2 70B (0.328 vs 0.345).

versions.untested_parts: No direction addition or direct measurement of refusal at every layer and position. Utility was assessed on benchmark accuracy, not every general ability.
Tests targeted parameter pruning, not a method specifically called abliteration; does not report an ablation-to-weight-edit pipeline on separately released models.
Whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or training against its ablation improves robustness.
Whether refusal is affine, cone-shaped, or composed of a dominant direction plus others.
Whether harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are encoded separately.
Tests directional ablation across model families and sizes; does not test transfer across languages or from base to instruct models.
How the timing or method of refusal training determines whether a removable direction exists.
Reasoning models that reason before answering.
